common_name: Winter Dreams Siebold Primrose (White Frilled Japanese Star Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring just as new growth emerges, into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, and mark the spot since the clump disappears completely below ground by midsummer.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled or partial shade, where clusters of pure white, deeply frilled flowers rise above softly wrinkled, hairy leaves each spring. 'Winter Dreams' forms slowly creeping clumps that are easy to combine with ferns and hostas in a woodland bed, filling gaps left by earlier spring ephemerals. Like other Japanese star primrose cultivars, it dies back completely by midsummer heat and reappears reliably the following spring, so avoid disturbing the dormant crown. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering and share increase, since named sieboldii cultivars do not come true from seed.

common_name: Snowflake Siebold Primrose (Heirloom White Fringed Japanese Star Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring before growth resumes, into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the dormant crown should be marked since it vanishes entirely once summer heat arrives.

directions: One of the oldest documented Japanese star primrose selections still in cultivation, 'Snowflake' bears clusters of pure white flowers with ragged, deeply cut petal edges above mid-green, crinkled foliage in mid-spring. It performs best in evenly moist, rich woodland soil in partial to full shade, where it slowly builds into a dense clump over several seasons. Expect the plant to go fully dormant by midsummer, a normal trait of the species that makes it a good companion for later-emerging shade perennials that can fill the space it leaves behind. Lift and divide overcrowded clumps in early spring to keep flowering strong and to propagate true copies, since this heirloom cultivar must be increased vegetatively.

common_name: Dancing Ladies Siebold Primrose (Fringed White-to-Pink Japanese Star Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring just before new growth appears, into humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist in partial to full shade, and mark the site since the plant dies back completely by summer.

directions: 'Dancing Ladies' carries smooth-petaled, finely fringed flowers that shift through shades of white to soft pink on erect stems held above pale green, wrinkled leaves covered in short hairs. Site it in moisture-retentive, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade alongside other sieboldii cultivars, where the varied flower tones create a soft, informal drift in mid-spring. The foliage fades and the plant disappears below ground as summer heat builds, a routine dormancy that is normal for the species and not a sign of poor health. Divide congested clumps in early spring every two to three years to maintain flowering vigor, since this cultivar is maintained only by division.

common_name: Chorister Show Auricula (Deep Yellow Gold-Centre Border Auricula)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade, ideally in a pot where overhead rain can be kept off the foliage and flowers.

directions: 'Chorister' is a deep yellow show auricula whose rounded petals surround a pure white, farina-dusted centre, held in neat trusses above thick, leathery, grey-green rosettes. Grow in gritty, loam-based compost that drains sharply yet never fully dries out, in bright but filtered light that avoids hot midday sun. Because the powdery farina on the foliage and flower centre washes off in rain, auricula enthusiasts traditionally grow show cultivars like this one in pots under a cold frame, alpine house, or auricula theatre rather than in open borders. Repot and divide offsets every one to two years after flowering to keep the rosettes vigorous and true to show form.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this hybrid tolerates heat and dry shade better than many epimediums once established.

directions: Low, dense rosettes of small, glossy, rounded leaflets flushed bronze in spring send up many erect racemes of cheerful, bright lemon-yellow bell-shaped flowers, held well above the foliage in a strong spring display. This hybrid closely resembles its wild parent but spreads more readily and shrugs off summer heat and dry shade with noticeably better constitution. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it slowly builds into a dense, weed-suppressing patch useful for underplanting trees and large shrubs. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges so the spring flower display is not obscured by tattered leaves.

common_name: Cranberry Sparkle Epimedium (Dark Cranberry-Red Large-Flowered Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this is a late-emerging, late-blooming selection so avoid disturbing the crown while it appears dormant in early spring.

directions: A wild selection originally found in the mountains of southern Japan, 'Cranberry Sparkle' carries unusually large, rich cranberry-red flowers held out almost horizontally on short stems, among the darkest-colored blooms found in the genus. Small leaflets emerge flushed with bronze in spring and mature to green, and the plant is notably slow to emerge and late to bloom compared with most grandiflorum selections, so patience is needed early in the season. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees once its root system is established. Cut back the previous year's foliage in late winter before new growth starts so the dramatic flowers are not hidden by old leaves.

common_name: Yokihi Epimedium (Late-Blooming Spidery Cream and Pink Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this is one of the latest epimediums to flower, so allow extra time before judging the display.

directions: A Japanese cross prized for its dramatic, spidery flowers, 'Yokihi' opens flared creamy-yellow cups with long, slender spurs backed by short, bright reddish-pink inner sepals, carried on arching stems well above the foliage. It is one of the latest epimediums to bloom each year, so its tight, semi-evergreen clump of angular leaflets flushed bronzy-red in spring rewards patience as the season progresses. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where established clumps are deer-resistant and tolerant of dry shade beneath trees. Groom away tattered old foliage in late winter so the unusual flower display is not obscured once the arching spikes emerge.
